# Overview



OpenFE is a comprehensive Python framework for alchemical free energy calculations in drug discovery. As the flagship project of the Open Free Energy consortium, it provides robust, permissively licensed open-source tools for molecular simulation workflows. The toolkit enables researchers to plan, execute, and analyze free energy calculations using various methods through both Python APIs and command-line interfaces.

## Architecture Overview

OpenFE follows a modular architecture built around three core pillars: **Setup**, **Protocols**, and **Analysis**. The framework leverages the `gufe` library for fundamental data structures and provides extensive OpenMM-based simulation protocols.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Core Framework"
        A[OpenFE Main Package]
        B[gufe - Core Data Structures]
        C[OpenMM - Simulation Engine]
    end
    
    subgraph "Setup Layer"
        D[Atom Mapping]
        E[Ligand Network Planning]
        F[Chemical System Generation]
    end
    
    subgraph "Protocol Layer"
        G[RBFE Protocols]
        H[ABFE Protocols]
        I[MD Protocols]
        J[Septop Methods]
    end
    
    subgraph "Interface Layer"
        K[Python API]
        L[Command Line Interface]
        M[Analysis Tools]
    end
    
    A --> B
    A --> C
    A --> D
    A --> E
    A --> F
    A --> G
    A --> H
    A --> I
    A --> J
    A --> K
    A --> L
    A --> M
```

## Key Components

### Setup Module
The setup module provides tools for preparing molecular systems and planning calculations:

- **Atom Mapping**: Multiple mapping algorithms including LomapAtomMapper, PersesAtomMapper, and KartografAtomMapper for determining correspondences between molecular structures [openfe/setup/__init__.py](openfe/setup/__init__.py#L5-L15)
- **Network Planning**: Algorithms for optimizing ligand transformation networks to minimize computational cost while maximizing accuracy
- **Chemical System Generation**: Tools for creating and validating molecular systems with proper components

### Protocol System
OpenFE implements a sophisticated protocol system for different types of free energy calculations:

| Protocol Type | Description | Key Features |
|---------------|-------------|--------------|
| **RBFE** | Relative Binding Free Energy | Ligand binding comparisons, network-based optimization |
| **ABFE** | Absolute Binding Free Energy | Single molecule binding calculations |
| **MD** | Molecular Dynamics | System equilibration and production runs |
| **Septop** | Restraint Methods | Advanced restraint systems for binding calculations |

The protocols are organized in the [openfe/protocols](openfe/protocols/) directory with specialized modules for each calculation type, all built on OpenMM for high-performance molecular simulations.

### Analysis and Visualization
OpenFE provides comprehensive tools for analyzing and visualizing results:

- **Network Analysis**: Maximum likelihood estimation for free energy networks
- **3D Visualization**: Molecular structure and transformation visualization
- **Plotting Tools**: Network graphs and result visualization capabilities

## Interface Options

OpenFE offers multiple ways to interact with the framework:

### Python API
The primary interface provides programmatic access to all OpenFE functionality:

```python
from openfe import LigandNetwork, Transformation
from openfe.setup import LomapAtomMapper, ligand_network_planning
```

### Command Line Interface
A comprehensive CLI ([openfecli/cli.py](openfecli/cli.py#L18-L25)) provides access to common operations through organized command sections:
- **Network Planning**: Tools for creating optimal ligand networks
- **Quickrun Executor**: Direct execution of calculations
- **Miscellaneous**: Utility functions and data management

## Project Structure

The toolkit follows a well-organized structure that separates concerns and maintains modularity:

![Project Structure](https://github.com/OpenFreeEnergy/openfe/blob/main/docs/_static/OFE-color-icon.svg?raw=true)

- **Core Package** ([openfe/](openfe/)): Main library with setup, protocols, analysis, and utilities
- **CLI Package** ([openfecli/](openfecli/)): Command-line interface and related tools
- **Documentation** ([docs/](docs/)): Comprehensive documentation with tutorials, guides, and API reference
- **Development Tools** ([devtools/](devtools/)): Scripts and utilities for development and testing

## Getting Started

OpenFE is designed to be accessible for beginners while providing advanced features for experts. The toolkit supports multiple installation methods including conda, Docker, and single-file installers. The project maintains high standards for code quality with comprehensive testing, documentation, and continuous integration.

**Next Steps**: For hands-on experience, proceed to [Quick Start](2-quick-start) to install OpenFE and run your first calculation, or visit [Installation and Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup) for detailed installation instructions.

# Quick Start



Welcome to OpenFE! This quick start guide will get you up and running with alchemical free energy calculations in minutes. OpenFE is a powerful, open-source toolkit for planning, executing, and analyzing molecular free energy calculations for drug discovery and computational chemistry.

## What You'll Accomplish

In this quick start, you will:
- Install OpenFE using the recommended method
- Verify your installation works correctly  
- Plan your first relative binding free energy (RBFE) network
- Execute a basic free energy calculation
- Understand the core OpenFE workflow

## System Requirements

Before we begin, ensure you have:
- **POSIX system** (macOS or Linux/Unix) - OpenFE is not currently compatible with Windows
- **Python 3.10+** (Python 3.11+ recommended for full functionality)
- **GPU support** (optional but recommended for performance)

## Installation

### The Recommended Way: Miniforge

We strongly recommend installing OpenFE with **Miniforge**, which provides easy installation of required dependencies like OpenMM and AmberTools.

```bash
# Install Miniforge (select your OS and architecture)
curl -OL https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
sh Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -b
~/miniforge3/bin/mamba init bash
```

After installation, restart your shell and create the OpenFE environment:

```bash
# Create and activate the OpenFE environment
mamba create -n openfe_env openfe
mamba activate openfe_env
```

### Verify Your Installation

Test that everything is working correctly:

```bash
# Quick test (takes a few seconds)
openfe test

# Comprehensive test (takes up to an hour, tests GPU features)
openfe test --long
```

> [!TIP]
> The first `openfe test` run may take longer due to code compilation, but this only happens once per installation.

## Core Architecture Overview

OpenFE follows a modular, network-based approach to free energy calculations:

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Molecules] --> B[Atom Mapping]
    B --> C[Network Planning]
    C --> D[Protocol Setup]
    D --> E[Simulation Execution]
    E --> F[Results Analysis]
    
    subgraph "Core Components"
        G[Chemical Systems]
        H[Transformations]
        I[Alchemical Networks]
    end
    
    subgraph "Execution Layer"
        J[Protocols]
        K[Protocol Units]
        L[Orchestration]
    end
```

The toolkit is built around these key concepts from the `gufe` library [openfe/__init__.py](openfe/__init__.py#L18-L30):
- **Chemical Systems**: Molecular representations (proteins, ligands, solvent)
- **Transformations**: Alchemical pathways between molecular states
- **Alchemical Networks**: Collections of interconnected transformations
- **Protocols**: Simulation execution methods (RBFE, ABFE, MD, etc.)

## Your First Calculation: CLI Workflow

Let's walk through a complete RBFE calculation using the command line interface.

### Step 1: Plan the Network

Create a relative binding free energy network for a set of ligands:

```bash
openfe plan-rbfe-network \
  --mol-dir path/to/ligands/ \
  --protein path/to/protein.pdb \
  --output-dir my_rbfe_network \
  --mapper lomap \
  --network-planner minimal-spanning-tree
```

This command:
- Reads ligands from the specified directory
- Maps atom correspondences using Lomap
- Plans an efficient network using minimal spanning tree algorithm
- Outputs the network configuration files

### Step 2: Execute the Calculation

Run the planned network using the quickrun executor:

```bash
openfe quickrun my_rbfe_network/transformation.json \
  --work-dir my_rbfe_results \
  --output results.json
```

The quickrun command [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L25-L42) executes the transformation defined in the JSON file, creating directories for each simulation task and storing the results.

### Step 3: Analyze Results

While detailed analysis is covered in later tutorials, you can quickly check your results:

```python
import json

# Load and examine results
with open('results.json', 'r') as f:
    results = json.load(f)
    
print(f"Free energy change: {results['free_energy']:.2f} kcal/mol")
```

## Your First Calculation: Python API Workflow

For more flexibility and customization, use the Python API:

```python
from openfe import SmallMoleculeComponent, ProteinComponent, SolventComponent
from openfe import LigandAtomMapper, LigandNetwork
from openfe.setup import lomap_scorers, ligand_network_planning
from openfe.protocols import OpenMM_RBFEProtocol

# Load molecular components
ligands = [SmallMoleculeComponent.from_file(f'ligand{i}.mol2') for i in range(5)]
protein = ProteinComponent.from_file('protein.pdb')
solvent = SolventComponent.from_file('solvent.xml')

# Create atom mapper and plan network
mapper = LigandAtomMapper()
scorer = lomap_scorers.default
network = ligand_network_planning.minimal_spanning_tree(ligands, mapper, scorer)

# Set up and execute protocol
protocol = OpenMM_RBFEProtocol(
    settings={'forcefield': 'openff-2.0.0', 'temperature': 300.0}
)

# Execute the first transformation
transformation = list(network.edges)[0]
results = protocol.execute(transformation)
print(f"ΔG = {results.get_free_energy():.2f} kcal/mol")
```

## Key Features at a Glance

| Feature | CLI | Python API | Use Case |
|---------|-----|------------|----------|
| **Network Planning** | ✅ | ✅ | Quick setup vs. custom control |
| **Protocol Selection** | ✅ | ✅ | Standard vs. custom protocols |
| **Batch Execution** | ✅ | ✅ | Simple scripts vs. orchestration |
| **Visualization** | Limited | ✅ | Basic vs. advanced plotting |
| **Customization** | Limited | ✅ | Standard workflows vs. research |

> [!TIP]
> Start with the CLI for quick calculations, then transition to the Python API for complex workflows and custom protocols.

## Installation Directory Structure

When you install OpenFE, you get both the core library and command line tools:

```
openfe/                    # Core Python library
├── protocols/             # Simulation protocols
├── setup/                # System setup tools
├── analysis/             # Results analysis
└── utils/                # Utility functions

openfecli/                 # Command line interface
├── commands/             # CLI commands
│   ├── plan_rbfe_network.py
│   ├── quickrun.py
│   └── ...
└── parameters/           # CLI parameter handling
```

## Common Quick Start Issues

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| **Import errors** | Ensure you've activated the conda environment: `mamba activate openfe_env` |
| **GPU not detected** | Install CUDA toolkit and check OpenMM GPU support: `python -c "from openmm import platform; print(platform.Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA').getName())"` |
| **Memory issues** | Reduce system size or use fewer parallel processes in your protocol settings |
| **Slow calculations** | Enable GPU acceleration and use appropriate sampling settings |

## Resources and Support

- **Documentation**: [https://docs.openfree.energy](https://docs.openfree.energy)
- **Example Notebooks**: [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/OpenFreeEnergy/ExampleNotebooks)

- **Community**: [Open Free Energy Website](https://openfree.energy)

You're now ready to explore the powerful world of alchemical free energy calculations with OpenFE! The toolkit provides both simplicity for beginners and flexibility for experts, making it an ideal choice for computational chemistry research and drug discovery applications.

# Installation and Environment Setup



OpenFE is a comprehensive Python package for executing alchemical free energy calculations, designed for both beginners and advanced users in computational chemistry and molecular modeling. This guide covers multiple installation approaches to suit different environments and use cases.

## System Requirements and Compatibility

OpenFE is currently compatible with POSIX systems (macOS and UNIX/Linux) and follows Scientific Python SPEC0 standards with specific considerations:

- **Python versions**: 3.10-3.14 supported (Python 3.10 no longer actively maintained as of openfe 1.6.0)
- **OpenMM versions**: 8.0, 8.1.2, 8.2.0 (OpenMM v8.3.0 not yet supported)
- **NAGL partial charges**: Requires Python ≥3.11
- **OpenEye Toolkits**: Not compatible with Python 3.13

## Supported Hardware Platforms

| Platform | Architecture | GPU Support | Recommendation |
|----------|--------------|-------------|----------------|
| Linux | x86_64, aarch64, ppc64le | NVIDIA CUDA | Production use |
| macOS | arm64 (Apple Silicon) | None | Development/testing |

For optimal performance, we recommend Linux x86_64 with NVIDIA GPUs and driver version 525.60.13 or greater.

## Installation Methods Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose Installation Method] --> B[Miniforge Recommended]
    A --> C[Existing Mamba/Conda]
    A --> D[Single File Installer]
    A --> E[Container Distribution]
    A --> F[Developer Install]
    
    B --> B1[Download Miniforge]
    B1 --> B2[Create Environment]
    B2 --> B3[Activate & Test]
    
    C --> C1[Use Existing Manager]
    C1 --> C2[Install openfe]
    C2 --> C3[Activate & Test]
    
    D --> D1[Download Installer]
    D1 --> D2[Run Installer]
    D2 --> D3[Verify Installation]
    
    E --> E1[Docker Pull]
    E1 --> E2[Apptainer Pull]
    E2 --> E3[Test GPU Access]
    
    F --> F1[Clone Repository]
    F1 --> F2[Create Environment]
    F2 --> F3[Editable Install]
```

## Installation with Miniforge (Recommended)

Miniforge provides the easiest installation experience with pre-configured conda-forge access and faster package resolution than conda.

### Step 1: Install Miniforge

Select your operating system, architecture, and shell from the interactive tool below, then run the generated commands:

```bash
# Example for Linux x86_64 with bash
curl -OL https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
sh Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -b
~/miniforge3/bin/mamba init bash
rm -f Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
```

### Step 2: Create OpenFE Environment

```bash
mamba create -n openfe_env openfe
mamba activate openfe_env
```

### Step 3: Verify Installation

```bash
# Quick test
openfe test

# Comprehensive test suite (recommended for production)
openfe test --long
```

> [!TIP]
> The first test run may take longer due to code compilation, but this only happens once per installation.

## Installation with Existing Mamba/Conda

If you already have mamba or micromamba installed:

```bash
mamba create -c conda-forge -n openfe_env openfe
mamba activate openfe_env
```

## Reproducible Builds with Conda-Lock

For cross-platform reproducible environments, use conda-lock files:

```bash
# Install conda-lock in separate environment
conda create -n conda-lock -c conda-lock
conda activate conda-lock

# Download latest lock file
curl -LOJ https://github.com/OpenFreeEnergy/openfe/releases/latest/download/openfe-conda-lock.yml

# Create environment from lock file
conda-lock install -n openfe openfe-conda-lock.yml
conda activate openfe

# Verify installation
pytest --pyargs openfe openfecli
```

## Single File Installer

For offline installations or when internet access is limited:

```bash
# Download installer (Linux x86_64 example)
curl -LOJ https://github.com/OpenFreeEnergy/openfe/releases/latest/download/OpenFEforge-Linux-x86_64.sh

# Make executable and run
chmod +x ./OpenFEforge-Linux-x86_64.sh
./OpenFEforge-Linux-x86_64.sh

# Verify installation
which python  # Should show openfeforge/bin/python
openfe --help
pytest --pyargs openfe openfecli
```

> [!TIP]
> The single file installer may modify your `.bashrc` and could require manual intervention to access previous conda installations.

## Containerized Distributions

### Docker

```bash
# Pull latest image
docker pull ghcr.io/openfreeenergy/openfe:latest

# For production, use specific version
docker pull ghcr.io/openfreeenergy/openfe:1.0.1
```

### Apptainer (Singularity)

```bash
# Pull image
singularity pull oras://ghcr.io/openfreeenergy/openfe:latest-apptainer

# Test GPU access
singularity run --nv openfe_latest-apptainer.sif python -m openmm.testInstallation

# Access CLI
singularity run --nv openfe_latest-apptainer.sif openfe --help
```

## HPC Environment Considerations

High Performance Computing environments present unique challenges due to differences between login and compute nodes. We recommend using containers for HPC deployments.

### CUDA Version Management

For conda-based installations in HPC environments:

```bash
# Check CUDA version on compute node
nvidia-smi  # Look for "CUDA Version" in output

# Override CUDA detection on login node
CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA=11.7 mamba create -n openfe_env openfe
```

### Virtual Package Detection

Conda uses virtual packages to detect system capabilities. The difference between login and compute nodes can cause issues:

```bash
# On login node (no GPU)
mamba info  # Shows: __archspec=1=x86_64, __glibc=2.17=0, __linux=3.10.0=0

# On compute node (with GPU)  
mamba info  # Shows: __archspec=1=x86_64, __cuda=11.7=0, __glibc=2.17=0
```

## Developer Installation

For contributing to OpenFE:

```bash
# Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/OpenFreeEnergy/openfe.git
cd openfe

# Create environment from specification
mamba create -f environment.yml
mamba activate openfe_env

# Install in editable mode
python -m pip install --no-deps -e .
```

## Optional Dependencies

Certain advanced features require additional packages:

```bash
# For perses tools (requires OpenEye license)
mamba install -c openeye perses openeye-toolkits
```

## Troubleshooting

### Debug Script

Run the debug script to diagnose installation issues:

```bash
bash -c "$(curl -Ls https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenFreeEnergy/openfe/main/devtools/debug_openmm.sh)" | tee -a debug.log
```

### Common Error: CUDA PTX Version Mismatch

```
openmm.OpenMMException: Error loading CUDA module: CUDA_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PTX_VERSION (222)
```

**Solution**: Re-create environment with correct CUDA toolkit version for your hardware/driver combination.

### Custom Docker Build Issues

When building custom Docker images, you may need to increase file descriptor limits:

```bash
docker build --ulimit nofile=262144:262144 .
```

## Environment Specification

The standard OpenFE environment includes these key dependencies:

- **Core**: OpenMM 8.2.0, OpenFF Toolkit, RDKit
- **Analysis**: pymbar, cinnabar, pandas  
- **Visualization**: py3dmol, networkx, pygraphviz
- **Testing**: pytest with parallel execution support
- **Documentation**: sphinx with pydata theme

For production deployments, the [production/environment.yml](production/environment.yml) provides a streamlined specification optimized for HPC environments.

## Next Steps

After successful installation, proceed to [Running Your First Free Energy Calculation](4-running-your-first-free-energy-calculation) to learn the basics of using OpenFE, or explore the [CLI Overview and Common Commands](5-cli-overview-and-common-commands) for command-line interface usage.

# Running Your First Free Energy Calculation



Welcome to your first free energy calculation with OpenFE! This guide will walk you through the complete process of setting up and running a relative binding free energy (RBFE) calculation using the command-line interface. RBFE calculations are fundamental in drug discovery for predicting how small modifications to ligands affect their binding affinity to a target protein.

## Understanding the OpenFE Workflow

Before diving into the practical steps, let's understand the high-level architecture of how OpenFE handles free energy calculations:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input Files<br/>Ligands + Protein] --> B[Network Planning<br/>plan-rbfe-network]
    B --> C[Charge Assignment<br/>AM1-BCC charges]
    C --> D[Atom Mapping<br/>Kartograf mapper]
    D --> E[Network Generation<br/>Minimal spanning network]
    E --> F[Protocol Setup<br/>OpenMM RBFE protocol]
    F --> G[JSON Output<br/>Transformation files]
    G --> H[Execution<br/>quickrun command]
    H --> I[Results Analysis<br/>ΔG values + uncertainties]
```

The workflow consists of two main phases: **planning** and **execution**. During planning, OpenFE analyzes your molecular system, generates atom mappings between ligands, and creates an optimized network of transformations. During execution, each transformation is simulated using molecular dynamics to calculate free energy differences.

## Prerequisites and Setup

Before running your first calculation, ensure you have:

1. **OpenFE installed** - Follow the [Installation and Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup) guide
2. **Molecular structure files**:
   - Ligand files in SDF format (or SMILES strings)
   - Protein structure in PDB or PDBx/mmCIF format
3. **Basic understanding** of free energy calculations (covered in [Alchemical Free Energy Calculations Fundamentals](6-alchemical-free-energy-calculations-fundamentals))

## Step 1: Prepare Your Input Files

### Ligand Files
OpenFE accepts ligands in multiple formats through the molecule loading system [openfecli/parameters/mol.py](openfecli/parameters/mol.py#L7-67):

- **SDF files** (recommended): Contains 3D coordinates and connectivity
- **MOL2 files**: Alternative format with partial charge information
- **SMILES strings**: Simple text representation for quick testing

```bash
# Example ligand files
ligands/
├── benzene.sdf
├── toluene.sdf
├── phenol.sdf
└── chlorobenzene.sdf
```

### Protein Files
Protein structures are loaded via the protein parameter system [openfecli/parameters/protein.py](openfecli/parameters/protein.py#L7-47):

- **PDB files**: Standard protein structure format
- **PDBx/mmCIF files**: Modern format with better handling of large structures

```bash
# Example protein file
protein/
└── tyrosine_kinase.pdb
```

> [!TIP]
> Ensure your protein structure is properly prepared: remove alternate conformations, add missing residues, and include all necessary cofactors. The quality of your input structures directly impacts calculation accuracy.

## Step 2: Plan Your RBFE Network

The `plan-rbfe-network` command is your gateway to setting up a complete free energy calculation campaign. This command handles all the complex setup automatically [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L75-257).

### Basic Command Structure

```bash
openfe plan-rbfe-network \
  --mol-dir ligands/ \
  --protein protein/tyrosine_kinase.pdb \
  --output-dir rbfe_network
```

### Key Parameters Explained

| Parameter | Required | Description | Default |
|-----------|----------|-------------|---------|
| `--mol-dir` | Yes | Directory containing ligand files | - |
| `--protein` | Yes | Protein structure file | - |
| `--cofactors` | No | Additional cofactor molecules | None |
| `--output-dir` | No | Output directory for network | `alchemicalNetwork` |
| `--n-protocol-repeats` | No | Number of simulation repeats | 3 |
| `--n-cores` | No | CPU cores for charge generation | 1 |

### What Happens During Planning?

1. **Charge Assignment**: OpenFE automatically generates AM1-BCC partial charges for all ligands using the OpenFF toolkit [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L85-95)

2. **Atom Mapping**: The KartografAtomMapper creates optimal correspondences between ligand atoms [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L25-27)

3. **Network Optimization**: A minimal spanning network is generated to minimize the total number of required transformations [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L27-29)

4. **Protocol Setup**: The OpenMM Relative Hybrid Topology Protocol is configured with default settings [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L70-75)

### Output Structure

After planning completes, you'll have:

```
rbfe_network/
├── transformation_1.json
├── transformation_2.json
├── transformation_3.json
└── ligand_network.json
```

Each JSON file contains a complete transformation ready for execution, including all simulation parameters and molecular system information.

## Step 3: Execute Your First Calculation

With your network planned, it's time to run the actual simulations using the `quickrun` command [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L25-142).

### Running a Single Transformation

```bash
openfe quickrun rbfe_network/transformation_1.json \
  --work-dir simulation_results \
  --output results_1.json
```

### Understanding the Execution Process

The `quickrun` command performs several key steps:

1. **DAG Creation**: Creates a directed acyclic graph of simulation tasks [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L85-87)
2. **Simulation Execution**: Runs molecular dynamics simulations for each lambda window [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L89-95)
3. **Result Analysis**: Processes simulation data to calculate free energy estimates [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L97-101)
4. **Error Handling**: Provides detailed error reporting if simulations fail [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L127-133)

### Expected Output

A successful calculation produces:

```json
{
  "estimate": -2.34,
  "uncertainty": 0.15,
  "protocol_result": {...},
  "unit_results": {...}
}
```

Where `estimate` is the ΔG value in kcal/mol and `uncertainty` represents the statistical error.

## Step 4: Analyze Your Results

### Understanding the Output

- **ΔG (estimate)**: Free energy difference between the two ligand states
- **Uncertainty**: Statistical confidence in the estimate
- **Protocol Result**: Detailed simulation metadata and convergence metrics

### Convergence Assessment

Good calculations typically show:
- Uncertainty < 0.5 kcal/mol for well-converged results
- Consistent results across multiple protocol repeats
- No large fluctuations in energy terms during simulation

### Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Issue | Likely Cause | Solution |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| High uncertainty (>1.0 kcal/mol) | Insufficient sampling time | Increase simulation length or protocol repeats |
| Simulation crashes | Poor atomic clashes in input | Check and prepare molecular structures |
| Large ΔG values (>10 kcal/mol) | Incorrect atom mapping | Verify ligand similarity and mapping quality |

## Advanced Options and Customization

### Custom Settings with YAML

For more control over your calculations, create a YAML settings file:

```yaml
mapper:
  type: KartografAtomMapper
  settings:
    atom_max_distance: 0.95
    map_hydrogens: true

scorer:
  type: default_lomap_scorer

network_planner:
  type: minimal_spanning_network

solvent:
  type: water
  ionic_strength: 0.15 M

partial_charge:
  partial_charge_method: am1bcc
  off_toolkit_backend: openeye
```

Use it with: `--settings custom_settings.yaml`

### High-Throughput Execution

For large ligand sets, consider:
- Using more CPU cores: `--n-cores 8`
- Parallel execution of multiple transformations
- Batch processing with job schedulers

## Next Steps

Congratulations! You've successfully run your first free energy calculation. To expand your knowledge:

1. **Explore different calculation types**: Learn about [Absolute Binding Free Energy (ABFE) Protocols](13-absolute-binding-free-energy-abfe-protocols)
2. **Deepen your understanding**: Study [Alchemical Free Energy Calculations Fundamentals](6-alchemical-free-energy-calculations-fundamentals)
3. **Master the CLI**: Read [CLI Overview and Common Commands](5-cli-overview-and-common-commands)
4. **Try Python interface**: Progress to the [RBFE Python Tutorial](tutorials/rbfe_python_tutorial.nblink) for programmatic control

> [!TIP]
> The command-line interface is perfect for getting started and routine calculations. As your needs grow, consider the Python API for greater flexibility and custom protocol development.

## Summary

You've now experienced the complete OpenFE workflow:

1. ✅ **Prepared** molecular input files
2. ✅ **Planned** an optimized RBFE network
3. ✅ **Executed** free energy simulations
4. ✅ **Analyzed** results and understood uncertainties

The OpenFE framework handles the complexity of free energy calculations while providing you with control over key parameters. This foundation enables you to tackle increasingly sophisticated molecular design challenges in drug discovery and computational chemistry.

# CLI Overview and Common Commands



The OpenFE Command Line Interface (CLI) provides a comprehensive set of tools for setting up, executing, and analyzing free energy calculations. This interface is designed to make common workflows accessible to both beginners and advanced users while maintaining the flexibility of the underlying Python library.

## CLI Architecture Overview

The CLI is organized into three main command categories, each serving distinct purposes in the free energy calculation workflow:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[OpenFE CLI] --> B[Network Planning]
    A --> C[Quickrun Executor]
    A --> D[Miscellaneous]
    
    B --> B1[plan-rbfe-network]
    B --> B2[plan-rhfe-network]
    B --> B3[view-ligand-network]
    
    C --> C1[quickrun]
    
    D --> D1[atommapping]
    D --> D2[charge-molecules]
    D --> D3[fetch]
    D --> D4[gather]
    D --> D5[test]
```

The main CLI entry point is defined in [openfecli/cli.py](openfecli/cli.py#L36-L45), which provides access to all subcommands through a unified interface. The command organization follows the logical workflow of free energy calculations: from network planning and setup through execution to results analysis.

## Network Planning Commands

### Relative Binding Free Energy (RBFE) Network Planning

The `plan-rbfe-network` command is the primary tool for setting up binding free energy calculations. This command automates the complex process of creating an optimal network of ligand transformations and preparing them for execution.

**Key Features:**
- Automatic ligand network optimization
- Partial charge generation for consistency across transformations
- Protocol configuration with customizable repeats
- Protein and cofactor handling

**Basic Usage:**
```bash
openfe plan-rbfe-network --molecules ./ligands/ --protein ./protein.pdb --output ./alchemicalNetwork
```

The command supports extensive customization through YAML configuration files and various parameters for mapper selection, scoring functions, and network planning algorithms [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L120-L144).

### Relative Hydration Free Energy (RHFE) Network Planning

For solvation free energy calculations, the `plan-rhfe-network` command provides similar functionality but focuses on vacuum-to-solvent transformations:

```bash
openfe plan-rhfe-network --molecules ./ligands/ --output ./hydrationNetwork
```

This tool is particularly useful for testing and validation purposes, offering a straightforward way to set up hydration free energy campaigns [openfecli/commands/plan_rhfe_network.py](openfecli/commands/plan_rhfe_network.py#L120-L135).

### Network Visualization

The `view-ligand-network` command allows you to visualize planned networks:

```bash
openfe view-ligand-network alchemicalNetwork/ligand_network.graphml
```

This generates visual representations of the transformation network, helping you understand the connectivity and optimization of your planned calculations [openfecli/commands/view_ligand_network.py](openfecli/commands/view_ligand_network.py#L6-L17).

## Execution Commands

### Quickrun Executor

The `quickrun` command executes individual transformations that have been planned by the network planning tools:

```bash
openfe quickrun alchemicalNetwork/transformation_1.json --work-dir ./run1 --output results1.json
```

This command handles the complete execution of a single transformation, including file management, result collection, and error handling [openfecli/commands/quickrun.py](openfecli/commands/quickrun.py#L17-L33).

> [!TIP]
> Quickrun automatically creates working directories and manages temporary files, ensuring clean execution environments for each transformation. Use the `--work-dir` option to specify custom locations for better organization of large calculation campaigns.

## Utility and Analysis Commands

### Atom Mapping Analysis

The `atommapping` command provides tools for examining and validating atom mappings between ligand pairs:

```bash
openfe atommapping --mol ligand1.sdf --mol ligand2.sdf --mapper kartograf --output mapping.png
```

This is essential for debugging mapping issues and understanding the correspondence between atoms in molecular transformations [openfecli/commands/atommapping.py](openfecli/commands/atommapping.py#L16-L29).

### Partial Charge Generation

The `charge-molecules` command generates partial charges for molecular sets:

```bash
openfe charge-molecules --molecules ./ligands/ --output charged_ligands.sdf --n-cores 4
```

This ensures consistent charge assignments across all molecules in a calculation network, which is critical for accurate free energy calculations [openfecli/commands/generate_partial_charges.py](openfecli/commands/generate_partial_charges.py#L30-L43).

### Results Gathering and Analysis

The `gather` command collects and analyzes results from multiple transformations:

```bash
openfe gather ./results/ --report ddg --output network_results.tsv
```

This powerful tool supports multiple analysis modes:
- `dg`: Maximum likelihood estimates of absolute ΔG values
- `ddg`: Relative binding free energies (ΔΔG)
- `raw`: Individual leg results for detailed analysis

The gather command automatically handles result validation, error detection, and statistical analysis across the entire network [openfecli/commands/gather.py](openfecli/commands/gather.py#L593-L640).

### Resource Management

The `fetch` command provides access to tutorials and example resources:

```bash
openfe fetch tutorial-rbfe
```

This downloads and sets up tutorial materials, making it easy to get started with OpenFE workflows [openfecli/commands/fetch.py](openfecli/commands/fetch.py#L51-L57).

### System Testing

The `test` command runs the OpenFE test suite to verify your installation:

```bash
openfe test --long
```

This comprehensive testing ensures that all components are functioning correctly in your environment [openfecli/commands/test.py](openfecli/commands/test.py#L12-L25).

## Common Command Patterns

| Workflow | Commands | Purpose |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **Complete RBFE Campaign** | `plan-rbfe-network` → `quickrun` → `gather` | Full binding free energy calculation |
| **Quick Mapping Check** | `atommapping` | Validate ligand transformations |
| **System Validation** | `test` → `fetch` → `charge-molecules` | Environment setup and testing |
| **Results Analysis** | `gather` → `view-ligand-network` | Post-calculation analysis and visualization |

## Parameter System

OpenFE CLI uses a sophisticated parameter system that provides type checking, validation, and help text generation. Common parameter types include:

- **MOL_DIR**: Directory containing molecular files
- **PROTEIN**: Protein structure file
- **OUTPUT_DIR**: Directory for calculation output
- **NCORES**: Number of processing cores
- **OVERWRITE**: File overwrite protection

These parameters ensure consistent behavior across commands and provide helpful error messages for incorrect usage.

> [!TIP]
> Most commands support YAML configuration files for advanced customization. Use the `--yaml-settings` option to specify custom mapper configurations, scoring functions, and protocol parameters without having to remember complex command-line arguments.

## Next Steps

After mastering these CLI basics, you may want to explore:

- [Running Your First Free Energy Calculation](4-running-your-first-free-energy-calculation) for a complete walkthrough
- [Alchemical Free Energy Calculations Fundamentals](6-alchemical-free-energy-calculations-fundamentals) for deeper theoretical understanding
- [Network-Based Molecular Transformations](7-network-based-molecular-transformations) for advanced network planning concepts

The CLI provides a solid foundation for free energy calculations, while the Python API offers additional flexibility for custom workflows and advanced research applications.

# Alchemical Free Energy Calculations Fundamentals



Alchemical free energy calculations form the theoretical and computational foundation of modern molecular design and drug discovery. This page introduces the fundamental concepts, methodologies, and implementation patterns used in OpenFE for performing alchemical transformations that predict binding free energies and molecular properties.

## Theoretical Foundations

### Thermodynamic Basis

Alchemical free energy calculations rely on the fundamental connection between free energy differences and statistical mechanics. The core principle involves computing the free energy difference ΔG between two thermodynamic states through a series of intermediate states that gradually transform one system into another. This approach leverages the fact that free energy is a state function, meaning the path taken between states does not affect the final result.

In OpenFE, this theoretical framework is implemented through the **AbsoluteAlchemicalFactory** class, which creates alchemically modified systems using **AlchemicalRegion** objects that define which atoms participate in the transformation [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L657-L662]. The factory systematically scales interactions using lambda (λ) parameters that control the gradual transformation from the initial to final state.

### Lambda Scheduling

The lambda schedule determines how the alchemical transformation is discretized into intermediate states. OpenFE implements separate lambda schedules for different interaction types:

- **Electrostatic interactions**: Scaled using `lambda_electrostatics`
- **Steric/van der Waals interactions**: Scaled using `lambda_sterics` 
- **Restraint forces**: Scaled using `lambda_restraints`

The scheduling is carefully designed with reversed lambda values (1-λ) to maintain consistency with the AbsoluteAlchemicalFactory convention where λ=1 represents fully interacting states [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L595-L597].

## Calculation Types

### Absolute Free Energy (AFE) Calculations

Absolute free energy calculations determine the free energy of transferring a molecule from one environment to another, typically from vacuum to solution or from solution to a binding site. The **BaseAbsoluteUnit** class provides the foundational framework for these calculations [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L86-L89].

Key components of AFE calculations include:

- **System preparation**: Creating the molecular system with appropriate solvent and protein components
- **Alchemical region definition**: Identifying atoms that will be decoupled/annihilated
- **Thermodynamic state generation**: Creating the series of intermediate lambda states
- **Simulation execution**: Running molecular dynamics at each lambda state
- **Free energy analysis**: Using MBAR (Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio) to compute final free energy differences

### Relative Free Energy (RFE) Calculations

Relative free energy calculations compute the difference in free energy between two similar molecules, typically evaluating relative binding affinities. The **RelativeHybridTopologyProtocol** implements these calculations using hybrid topology approaches [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L496-L496].

RFE calculations in OpenFE support multiple sampling methods:

- **Hamiltonian Replica Exchange (HREX)**: Exchanges configurations between different lambda states
- **Self-adjusted mixture sampling (SAMS)**: Adapts sampling weights for optimal efficiency
- **Independent window sampling**: Simulates each lambda state independently

> [!TIP]
> Relative calculations are generally more accurate than absolute calculations because systematic errors cancel out when computing differences between similar molecules. This makes RFE the preferred approach for most drug discovery applications.

## System Preparation and Validation

### Component Management

OpenFE uses a modular component-based system where molecules are represented as **Component** objects:

- **SmallMoleculeComponent**: Represents drug-like molecules with defined chemistry
- **ProteinComponent**: Represents protein structures with proper residue definitions  
- **SolventComponent**: Defines the solvent environment (water model, ionic strength)

The system preparation process involves assigning partial charges to molecules using methods like AM1-BCC or RESP charges [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L400-L404], creating the molecular topology, and placing components in an appropriate simulation box.

### Alchemical Region Definition

The alchemical region specifies which atoms participate in the transformation. For absolute calculations, this typically involves decoupling an entire ligand from its environment. For relative calculations, the region includes atoms that differ between the two ligands.

The **_get_alchemical_indices** method identifies these atoms by examining the component residues and topology information [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L135-L141], ensuring that only the intended atoms are modified during the alchemical transformation.

## Simulation and Analysis

### Multi-State Sampling

OpenFE implements multi-state sampling using the **MultiStateSampler** framework from OpenMMTools. This approach simultaneously simulates multiple lambda states, allowing for efficient exchange of configurations between states and improved statistical sampling.

The **MultistateEquilFEAnalysis** class provides comprehensive analysis tools for evaluating simulation results [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/multistate_analysis.py#L62-L87]. Key analysis capabilities include:

- **Equilibration detection**: Automatically identifying when simulations reach equilibrium
- **Free energy calculation**: Using MBAR to compute free energy differences with uncertainty estimates
- **Overlap matrix analysis**: Evaluating phase space overlap between lambda states
- **Replica exchange statistics**: Monitoring the efficiency of state exchanges

### Adaptive Protocol Settings

OpenFE includes intelligent protocol adaptation based on system characteristics. The **_adaptive_settings** method automatically adjusts simulation parameters for challenging transformations [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L548-L614]:

```python
# Example: Charge-changing transformations get enhanced settings
if mapping.get_alchemical_charge_difference() != 0:
    protocol_settings.simulation_settings.production_length = 20 * unit.nanosecond
    protocol_settings.simulation_settings.n_replicas = 22
    protocol_settings.lambda_settings.lambda_windows = 22
```

> [!TIP]
> Charge-changing transformations require more careful sampling due to the long-range nature of electrostatic interactions. OpenFE automatically detects these cases and applies enhanced protocols with increased simulation time and more lambda windows.

## Quality Assurance and Validation

### Convergence Assessment

Proper convergence assessment is critical for reliable free energy calculations. OpenFE provides multiple metrics for evaluating convergence:

- **Statistical uncertainty**: Bootstrap analysis provides confidence intervals
- **Forward-reverse consistency**: Comparing forward and reverse transformation results
- **Overlap matrix eigenvalues**: Ensuring adequate phase space overlap between states
- **Replica exchange acceptance rates**: Monitoring sampling efficiency

The **get_forward_and_reverse_analysis** method implements comprehensive convergence checks by analyzing subsets of the trajectory data [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/multistate_analysis.py#L284-L286].

### Error Estimation

Free energy uncertainties are estimated using MBAR's statistical framework combined with bootstrap resampling. The **_get_free_energy** method implements this analysis, providing both point estimates and confidence intervals [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/multistate_analysis.py#L199-L205].

## Integration with Network-Based Approaches

OpenFE is designed around the concept of **alchemical networks**, where multiple transformations are organized into connected graphs. This network-based approach enables:

- **Redundant pathways**: Multiple routes between molecules improve robustness
- **Cycle closure analysis**: Internal consistency checks within the network
- **Maximum likelihood estimation**: Global optimization across all network edges

The **AbstractAlchemicalNetworkPlanner** provides the interface for creating these networks [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/abstract_alchemical_network_planner.py#L9-L16], with concrete implementations for different planning strategies.

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the fundamentals of alchemical free energy calculations, you can explore:

- [Network-Based Molecular Transformations](7-network-based-molecular-transformations) to learn how multiple calculations are organized into efficient networks
- [Protocol System and Execution Framework](8-protocol-system-and-execution-framework) to understand the computational infrastructure
- [Atom Mapping and Molecular Transformations](9-atom-mapping-and-molecular-transformations) for detailed information about preparing molecular transformations

The modular design of OpenFE allows you to start with simple absolute calculations and progress to complex network-based relative binding free energy studies as you become more familiar with the framework.

# Network-Based Molecular Transformations



Network-based molecular transformations represent a fundamental paradigm in computational chemistry where free energy calculations are organized as interconnected graphs rather than isolated pairwise comparisons. This approach enables efficient exploration of chemical space through strategic pathway planning, error cancellation, and thermodynamic cycle closure.

## Core Architecture

The OpenFE framework implements network-based transformations through a hierarchical architecture that separates concerns between ligand network planning, chemical system generation, and protocol execution. The foundation rests on the `AbstractAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` interface [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/abstract_alchemical_network_planner.py#L9](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/abstract_alchemical_network_planner.py#L9), which defines the contract for all network planning implementations.

### Network Planning Hierarchy

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[AbstractAlchemicalNetworkPlanner] --> B[RelativeAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    B --> C[RBFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    B --> D[RHFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    
    E[Ligand Network Planning] --> F[generate_minimal_spanning_network]
    E --> G[generate_radial_network]
    E --> H[generate_maximal_network]
    E --> I[generate_minimal_redundant_network]
    
    J[Chemical System Generation] --> K[EasyChemicalSystemGenerator]
    
    L[Protocol Execution] --> M[RelativeHybridTopologyProtocol]
```

The `RelativeAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` serves as the concrete implementation base [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L46](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L46), orchestrating three key components:

1. **Ligand Mappers**: Tools for establishing atom correspondence between molecules
2. **Mapping Scorers**: Functions evaluating transformation quality and feasibility  
3. **Network Planners**: Algorithms optimizing the graph topology for computational efficiency

## Network Planning Strategies

OpenFE provides multiple network generation algorithms, each optimized for different computational scenarios:

### Minimal Spanning Network

The `generate_minimal_spanning_network` function creates the most computationally efficient topology by connecting all ligands with the minimum number of edges while maximizing total mapping scores [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L208](openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L208). This approach minimizes computational cost while maintaining connectivity through high-quality transformations.

### Radial Network

The radial (hub-and-spoke) topology centers all transformations around a single reference ligand [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L49](openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L49). This strategy provides consistent reference points and simplifies analysis, making it ideal for lead optimization campaigns where all compounds are compared to a common scaffold.

### Maximal Network

For comprehensive exploration, the `generate_maximal_network` generates all possible pairwise mappings [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L157](openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L157). While computationally intensive, this approach maximizes pathway redundancy and provides the most robust error cancellation through cycle closure.

## Specialized Network Planners

### Relative Binding Free Energy (RBFE) Networks

The `RBFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` specializes in protein-ligand binding calculations [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L289](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L289). Key features include:

- **Adaptive Protocol Settings**: Automatic adjustment of simulation parameters based on transformation characteristics
- **Net Charge Handling**: Specialized treatment for transformations involving charge changes
- **Protein Context Integration**: Proper handling of protein-ligand complex formation and solvent effects

The planner accepts ligands, solvent, protein, and optional cofactors to construct complete binding thermodynamic cycles [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L350](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L350).

### Relative Hydration Free Energy (RHFE) Networks

The `RHFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` focuses on solvation thermodynamics by comparing ligand binding in solvent versus vacuum [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L225](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L225). This approach enables:

- **Solvation Energy Decomposition**: Separation of binding and desolvation contributions
- **Vacuum Simulations**: Specialized handling of non-periodic boundary conditions
- **Transferability Assessment**: Evaluation of ligand properties across different environments

> [!TIP]
> The chemical system generator automatically configures vacuum simulations with "nocutoff" nonbonded methods when detecting transformations involving vacuum states, ensuring proper treatment of long-range electrostatics.

## Transformation Construction

Each network edge represents a molecular transformation with associated thermodynamic protocols. The transformation construction process involves:

1. **Mapping Generation**: Atom correspondence establishment through configurable mappers
2. **System Preparation**: Chemical system generation for both endpoint states
3. **Protocol Assignment**: Simulation protocol configuration and parameter adaptation
4. **Network Assembly**: Integration of individual transformations into a coherent graph

The framework supports protocol adaptation based on transformation characteristics, particularly for charge-changing mutations where simulation parameters require special consideration [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L314](openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L314).

## Integration and Extensibility

The network-based architecture seamlessly integrates with OpenFE's broader ecosystem:

- **Storage Systems**: Network metadata and results are managed through specialized storage clients
- **Analysis Tools**: Network-wide analysis enables thermodynamic cycle validation and error estimation
- **Visualization Utilities**: Network plotting capabilities provide insight into transformation pathways and computational efficiency

> [!TIP]
> The modular design allows users to mix and match mappers, scorers, and network planners to create customized workflows optimized for specific chemical systems and computational resources.

## Practical Applications

Network-based transformations excel in scenarios requiring:

- **Lead Optimization**: Efficient exploration of structure-activity relationships through targeted networks
- **Selectivity Studies**: Comparative analysis across multiple protein targets
- **Property Prediction**: Systematic evaluation of physicochemical properties across chemical series
- **Method Validation**: Thermodynamic cycle closure provides internal consistency checks

The network approach transforms individual free energy calculations into a coherent thermodynamic framework, enabling more robust predictions and deeper chemical insights than isolated pairwise comparisons.

For detailed implementation guidance, see [Atom Mapping and Molecular Transformations](9-atom-mapping-and-molecular-transformations) and [Ligand Network Planning Algorithms](10-ligand-network-planning-algorithms). Protocol-specific details are covered in [Relative Binding Free Energy (RBFE) Protocols](12-relative-binding-free-energy-rbfe-protocols) and [Absolute Binding Free Energy (ABFE) Protocols](13-absolute-binding-free-energy-abfe-protocols).

# Protocol System and Execution Framework



The OpenFE protocol system provides a comprehensive, extensible framework for executing free energy calculations through a well-architected hierarchy of protocols, units, and settings. This framework enables reproducible, scalable computational chemistry workflows while maintaining flexibility for custom method development.

## Architecture Overview

The protocol system follows a layered architecture that separates concerns between high-level workflow orchestration, specific calculation protocols, and detailed simulation settings. This design enables both ease of use for standard workflows and extensibility for advanced users.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Protocol Layer"
        A[gufe.Protocol] --> B[RelativeHybridTopologyProtocol]
        A --> C[AbsoluteBindingProtocol]
        A --> D[Custom Protocols]
    end
    
    subgraph "Execution Layer"
        E[gufe.ProtocolUnit] --> F[BaseAbsoluteUnit]
        E --> G[RelativeHybridTopologyProtocolUnit]
        E --> H[AbsoluteBindingComplexUnit]
        E --> I[AbsoluteBindingSolventUnit]
    end
    
    subgraph "Settings Layer"
        J[SettingsBaseModel] --> K[Protocol-Specific Settings]
        K --> L[MultiStateSimulationSettings]
        K --> M[OpenMMEngineSettings]
        K --> N[IntegratorSettings]
    end
    
    subgraph "Utility Layer"
        O[LambdaProtocol] --> P[Alchemical State Management]
        Q[OpenMM Utils] --> R[System Generation & Validation]
        S[Restraint Utils] --> T[Geometry & Force Application]
    end
    
    B --> G
    C --> H
    C --> I
    G --> P
    H --> P
    I --> P
    G --> R
    H --> R
    I --> R
    H --> T
```

## Core Protocol Classes

### Relative Free Energy Protocols

The `RelativeHybridTopologyProtocol` [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L496](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L496) implements ligand-to-ligand transformations using hybrid topology systems. This protocol supports multiple sampling methods including Hamiltonian Replica Exchange, Self-Adjusted Mixture Sampling, and Independent Window Sampling.

Key features include:
- **Hybrid topology construction** for seamless alchemical transformations
- **Multi-state sampling** with configurable replica exchange strategies
- **Comprehensive analysis** including overlap matrices and replica transition statistics
- **Adaptive settings** that automatically configure parameters based on molecular properties

The protocol creates `RelativeHybridTopologyProtocolUnit` instances [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L683](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L683) that execute individual transformations, with results aggregated in `RelativeHybridTopologyProtocolResult` [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L276](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_methods.py#L276).

### Absolute Free Energy Protocols

The `AbsoluteBindingProtocol` [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L517](openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L517) handles ligand binding calculations through separate complex and solvent phases. This protocol builds on the `BaseAbsoluteUnit` [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L86](openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L86) which provides common functionality for absolute calculations.

The protocol creates two distinct unit types:
- **Complex phase**: `AbsoluteBindingComplexUnit` [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L914](openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L914) for bound state simulations
- **Solvent phase**: `AbsoluteBindingSolventUnit` [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L1262](openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/equil_binding_afe_method.py#L1262) for unbound state simulations

Both phases incorporate Boresch restraints for proper standard state corrections and provide detailed structural analysis capabilities.

## Settings and Configuration

### Hierarchical Settings System

The protocol framework uses a sophisticated settings hierarchy based on `SettingsBaseModel` that provides type validation, default values, and comprehensive documentation:

| Settings Class | Primary Purpose | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `MultiStateSimulationSettings` [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L544](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L544) | Alchemical sampling control | `sampler_method`, `n_replicas`, `time_per_iteration` |
| `OpenMMEngineSettings` [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L314](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L314) | MD engine configuration | `compute_platform`, `gpu_device_index` |
| `IntegratorSettings` [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L353](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L353) | Integration parameters | `timestep`, `langevin_collision_rate` |
| `OpenMMSolvationSettings` [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L50](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L50) | System solvation | `solvent_model`, `solvent_padding` |

### Protocol-Specific Settings

Each protocol defines specialized settings classes that inherit from the base settings:

- **Lambda Settings**: Control alchemical switching functions and window distributions [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_settings.py#L33](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_settings.py#L33)
- **Alchemical Settings**: Configure soft-core potentials and charge handling [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_settings.py#L50](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/equil_rfe_settings.py#L50)
- **Partial Charge Settings**: Manage charge calculation methods and backends [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L231](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/omm_settings.py#L231)

> [!TIP]
> The settings system uses Pydantic models with automatic validation, ensuring that invalid configurations are caught early with clear error messages. This prevents common mistakes like incompatible timestep values or unsupported sampling methods.

## Lambda Protocol System

### Alchemical State Management

The `LambdaProtocol` class [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L14](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L14) provides sophisticated control over alchemical transformations through configurable switching functions. It manages the progression of different energy components (electrostatics, sterics) throughout the transformation pathway.

Key capabilities include:
- **Multiple switching functions** with customizable parameters
- **Charge singularity avoidance** through naked charge detection [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L231](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L231)
- **Visualization tools** for lambda schedule inspection and validation

The `RelativeAlchemicalState` [openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L291](openfe/protocols/openmm_rfe/_rfe_utils/lambdaprotocol.py#L291) extends this framework with specific parameters for relative transformations, handling insertion/deletion processes and core component scaling.

## Execution and Orchestration

### Protocol Unit Execution

Protocol units implement the core execution logic through standardized interfaces:

1. **Preparation Phase**: System setup, charge assignment, and topology construction
2. **Equilibration Phase**: Energy minimization and gradual system relaxation
3. **Production Phase**: Alchemical sampling with configured methods
4. **Analysis Phase**: Result processing and statistical analysis

The `BaseAbsoluteUnit` [openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L86](openfe/protocols/openmm_afe/base.py#L86) provides a template method pattern that standardizes this workflow while allowing customization at each stage.

### Result Management

Protocol results implement comprehensive analysis interfaces:

- **Free Energy Estimation**: MBAR-based analysis with uncertainty quantification
- **Overlap Assessment**: Matrix-based evaluation of sampling efficiency
- **Replica Analysis**: Transition statistics and state distribution monitoring
- **Structural Analysis**: Trajectory inspection and restraint geometry validation

> [!TIP]
> Results are stored in structured formats that enable both immediate analysis and post-processing. The system maintains full provenance information, allowing traceability from final results back to original input parameters.

## Extension Framework

### Custom Protocol Development

The framework supports extension through well-defined interfaces:

1. **Protocol Subclassing**: Inherit from `gufe.Protocol` for new calculation types
2. **Unit Implementation**: Create specialized `ProtocolUnit` classes for execution logic
3. **Settings Definition**: Design configuration classes using `SettingsBaseModel`
4. **Result Handling**: Implement `ProtocolResult` for output management

### Utility Integration

The protocol system integrates with specialized utility modules:
- **OpenMM Utils** [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/): System generation and validation
- **Restraint Utils** [openfe/protocols/restraint_utils/](openfe/protocols/restraint_utils/): Geometry management and force application
- **Charge Generation** [openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/charge_generation.py](openfe/protocols/openmm_utils/charge_generation.py): Partial charge calculation workflows

This modular architecture enables rapid development of new methods while leveraging existing, validated components.

## Next Steps

To deepen your understanding of the protocol system:

- Explore [Relative Binding Free Energy (RBFE) Protocols](12-relative-binding-free-energy-rbfe-protocols) for specific implementation details
- Review [Absolute Binding Free Energy (ABFE) Protocols](13-absolute-binding-free-energy-abfe-protocols) for complex transformation workflows
- Study [Custom Protocol Development](20-custom-protocol-development) for extension guidance
- Examine [High-Throughput Execution and Orchestration](22-high-throughput-execution-and-orchestration) for scaling considerations

The protocol system serves as the foundation for reproducible free energy calculations, providing both the flexibility needed for research and the robustness required for production workflows.

# Atom Mapping and Molecular Transformations



Atom mapping is a fundamental process in free energy calculations that establishes correspondence between atoms in different molecular states. This process enables the construction of alchemical pathways where molecules are gradually transformed from one state to another, allowing for the computation of relative free energy differences.

## Core Architecture

The atom mapping system in OpenFE is built around an extensible architecture that supports multiple mapping algorithms and scoring functions. The foundation is the `LigandAtomMapper` abstract base class, which defines the interface for generating atom correspondences between `SmallMoleculeComponent` instances [ligandatommapper.py#L11-L17].

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class LigandAtomMapper {
        <<abstract>>
        +suggest_mappings(componentA, componentB)
        +_mappings_generator(componentA, componentB)*
    }
    
    class LomapAtomMapper {
        +_mappings_generator()
    }
    
    class PersesAtomMapper {
        +allow_ring_breaking: bool
        +preserve_chirality: bool
        +use_positions: bool
        +coordinate_tolerance: Quantity
        +_mappings_generator()
    }
    
    class KartografAtomMapper {
        +_mappings_generator()
    }
    
    LigandAtomMapper <|-- LomapAtomMapper
    LigandAtomMapper <|-- PersesAtomMapper
    LigandAtomMapper <|-- KartografAtomMapper
```

## Implementation Classes

### Base Mapper Interface

The `LigandAtomMapper` class serves as the foundation for all mapping implementations. It requires subclasses to implement the `_mappings_generator` method, which returns an iterable of atom mapping dictionaries [ligandatommapper.py#L19-L38]. The public `suggest_mappings` method converts these dictionaries into `LigandAtomMapping` objects [ligandatommapper.py#L40-L65].

### Lomap Integration

The `LomapAtomMapper` provides a wrapper around the Lomap library's maximum common substructure (MCS) algorithm. This mapper is imported directly from the Lomap package and adapted to match OpenFE's API [lomap_mapper.py#L9].

### Perses Integration

The `PersesAtomMapper` offers sophisticated mapping capabilities with configurable parameters:

- **allow_ring_breaking**: Controls whether only full molecular cycles should be mapped
- **preserve_chirality**: Enforces strict chirality preservation in mappings
- **use_positions**: Utilizes spatial coordinates for mapping decisions
- **coordinate_tolerance**: Defines the distance tolerance for position-based mapping [perses_mapper.py#L52-L80]

The implementation constructs a Perses `AtomMapper` and processes the resulting mappings, with optional chirality preservation [perses_mapper.py#L82-L110].

## Scoring Systems

OpenFE provides comprehensive scoring functions to evaluate the quality of atom mappings:

### Lomap Scorers

The Lomap scoring suite includes multiple specialized metrics [lomap_scorers.py#L4-L16]:
- `atomic_number_score`: Evaluates atomic number consistency
- `default_lomap_score`: Standard Lomap scoring function
- `ecr_score`: Edge consistency ratio scoring
- `heterocycles_score`: Heterocycle mapping quality
- `hybridization_score`: Hybridization state preservation
- `mcsr_score`, `mncar_score`, `tmcsr_score`: Various substructure matching scores

### Perses Scorer

The `default_perses_scorer` provides normalized scoring with optional position-based evaluation [perses_scorers.py#L37-L121]. It considers multiple factors:
- Number of mapped atoms
- Aromatic atom correspondence
- Heavy atom mapping quality
- Ring structure preservation

> [!TIP]
> The Perses scorer normalization uses weighted combinations of different mapping aspects (1.0 for total atoms, 0.8 for aromatic, 0.5 for heavy atoms, 0.4 for ring atoms) to enable cross-comparison between different molecular pairs [perses_scorers.py#L111-L117].

## Command Line Interface

The atom mapping functionality is accessible through the `openfe atommapping` command, which provides tools for examining specific mappings between ligand pairs [atommapping.py#L16-L40].

### Usage Patterns

The CLI supports two main output modes:

1. **Dictionary Output**: Prints the atom mapping correspondence directly to console [atommapping.py#L68-L71]
2. **Visualization**: Generates PNG images showing the mapped molecular structures [atommapping.py#L74-L97]

The command requires exactly two molecules and a mapper specification, using the `generate_mapping` utility to ensure single mapping results [atommapping.py#L43-L65].

## Integration with Alchemical Networks

Atom mappings serve as the foundation for molecular transformations in alchemical networks. Each mapping defines a specific transformation pathway between two molecular states, enabling the systematic construction of free energy calculation networks.

The mapping quality directly impacts the reliability and efficiency of subsequent free energy calculations. High-quality mappings with good chemical intuition and minimal structural perturbations lead to more accurate and convergent simulations.

> [!TIP]
> When selecting a mapper for your workflow, consider the trade-off between mapping coverage and quality. Lomap typically provides faster, more conservative mappings, while Perses offers more sophisticated position-aware mapping at the cost of increased computational complexity.

## Next Steps

After establishing atom mappings, you can explore [Ligand Network Planning Algorithms](10-ligand-network-planning-algorithms) to understand how individual mappings are combined into comprehensive alchemical networks, or proceed to [Chemical System Generation and Validation](11-chemical-system-generation-and-validation) to learn about preparing molecular systems for simulation.

# Ligand Network Planning Algorithms



Ligand network planning algorithms are fundamental to OpenFE's approach to relative free energy calculations. These algorithms determine how ligands are connected in a network, directly impacting computational efficiency, accuracy, and statistical robustness of the calculations. The system provides multiple network planning strategies optimized for different use cases, from minimal computational footprint to maximum redundancy.

## Network Planning Architecture

The ligand network planning system follows a hierarchical architecture that separates concerns between network topology generation and alchemical transformation creation. At the core is the `AbstractAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` interface [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/abstract_alchemical_network_planner.py#L9-L16], which defines the contract for all network planners. The concrete implementation `RelativeAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L46] serves as the base for specialized planners like `RBFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` and `RHFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner`.

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[AbstractAlchemicalNetworkPlanner] --> B[RelativeAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    B --> C[RBFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    B --> D[RHFEAlchemicalNetworkPlanner]
    
    E[Ligand Network Planning Functions] --> F[generate_radial_network]
    E --> G[generate_maximal_network]
    E --> H[generate_minimal_spanning_network]
    E --> I[generate_minimal_redundant_network]
    
    B --> E
    C --> J[Protein + Solvent Systems]
    D --> K[Solvent Only Systems]
```

The planner orchestrates three key components: atom mappers for proposing molecular correspondences, scoring functions for evaluating mapping quality, and network planning algorithms for optimizing the graph topology [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L49-L95].

## Core Network Planning Algorithms

### Minimal Spanning Network

The `generate_minimal_spanning_network` function creates the most computationally efficient network by connecting all ligands with the minimum number of edges while maximizing total mapping scores [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L208-L235]. This approach uses a minimum spanning tree algorithm to ensure every ligand is reachable while minimizing computational cost.

**Key characteristics:**
- **Edge count**: N-1 edges for N ligands
- **Optimization**: Maximizes total mapping score
- **Use case**: Limited computational resources, initial screening

### Radial Network

The radial network (also known as hub-and-spoke or star-map) connects all ligands through a central reference ligand [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L49-L120]. This topology is particularly useful when you have a well-characterized reference compound or want to minimize error propagation through the network.

**Key characteristics:**
- **Edge count**: N-1 edges (all connected to central hub)
- **Central ligand**: Can be specified by name, index, or molecule object
- **Advantage**: Reduces cumulative errors,便于结果解释

### Maximal Network

The `generate_maximal_network` function creates a complete network with all possible ligand-to-ligand connections [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L157-L207]. This comprehensive approach generates up to N(N-1)/2 potential edges, making it ideal for debugging atom mappers or as a starting point for other optimization algorithms.

**Key characteristics:**
- **Edge count**: Up to N(N-1)/2 edges
- **Completeness**: Includes all possible mappings
- **Use case**: Mapper debugging, comprehensive analysis

### Minimal Redundant Network

The `generate_minimal_redundant_network` provides a balance between efficiency and statistical robustness by ensuring each node has multiple connections [openfe/setup/ligand_network_planning.py#L252-L295]. This algorithm generates multiple minimum spanning trees to provide redundancy while maintaining computational efficiency.

**Key characteristics:**
- **Redundancy level**: Controlled by `mst_num` parameter
- **Statistical robustness**: Multiple paths between ligands
- **Error estimation**: Enables uncertainty quantification

## Algorithm Selection Guidelines

| Algorithm | Computational Cost | Statistical Robustness | Error Propagation | Best Use Case |
|-----------|-------------------|------------------------|-------------------|---------------|
| Minimal Spanning | Lowest | Low | High | Resource-constrained screening |
| Radial | Low | Medium | Low | Reference-based studies |
| Maximal | Highest | High | Low | Mapper debugging, analysis |
| Minimal Redundant | Medium | High | Medium | Production calculations |

## Integration with Alchemical Planning

The network planning algorithms integrate seamlessly with the broader alchemical planning framework. The `RelativeAlchemicalNetworkPlanner` uses the specified network planner to generate ligand connections, then constructs full alchemical transformations by combining these with chemical systems and protocols [openfe/setup/alchemical_network_planner/relative_alchemical_network_planner.py#L121-L140].

> [!TIP]
> The choice of network planner significantly impacts both computational efficiency and result accuracy. For production calculations, consider using minimal redundant networks with mst_num=2 to balance cost and statistical robustness.

## Command Line Interface

OpenFE provides CLI commands for network planning, including `plan-rbfe-network` and `plan-rhfe-network` [openfecli/commands/plan_rbfe_network.py#L120-L144]. These commands expose the network planning functionality through a user-friendly interface, supporting various mappers, scorers, and network planning algorithms.

## Advanced Configuration

Network planners support advanced configuration through:
- **Multiple mappers**: Combine different mapping strategies
- **Custom scoring functions**: Implement domain-specific mapping evaluation
- **Parallel processing**: Leverage multiple cores for large ligand sets
- **Progress tracking**: Monitor network generation for large systems

The system's modular design allows easy extension with new network planning algorithms while maintaining compatibility with existing workflows. This flexibility enables researchers to tailor network topology to their specific computational constraints and accuracy requirements.

> [!TIP]
> When working with charged ligands, ensure your mapper supports element changes and charge variations. The default LomapAtomMapper configuration includes element_change=True for this purpose.

For understanding how these networks integrate with molecular transformations, see [Atom Mapping and Molecular Transformations](9-atom-mapping-and-molecular-transformations). To learn about executing calculations on planned networks, refer to [Protocol System and Execution Framework](8-protocol-system-and-execution-framework).

# Chemical System Generation and Validation



Chemical system generation and validation in OpenFE provides a systematic framework for creating consistent molecular environments for free energy calculations. This module ensures that ligands are properly prepared across different simulation scenarios including vacuum, solvent, and protein-bound states.

## Architecture Overview

The chemical system generation framework follows an abstract factory pattern with a concrete implementation for common use cases. The architecture is built around standardized component labels and a flexible generator system that can handle various molecular environments.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class AbstractChemicalSystemGenerator {
        <<abstract>>
        +__call__(component) Iterable~ChemicalSystem~
    }
    
    class EasyChemicalSystemGenerator {
        -solvent: SolventComponent
        -protein: ProteinComponent
        -cofactors: List~SmallMoleculeComponent~
        -do_vacuum: bool
        +__init__(solvent, protein, cofactors, do_vacuum)
        +__call__(component) Iterable~ChemicalSystem~
    }
    
    class RFEComponentLabels {
        <<enumeration>>
        PROTEIN: "protein"
        LIGAND: "ligand"
        SOLVENT: "solvent"
        COFACTOR: "cofactor"
    }
    
    class ChemicalSystem {
        +components: Dict
        +name: str
    }
    
    AbstractChemicalSystemGenerator <|-- EasyChemicalSystemGenerator
    EasyChemicalSystemGenerator --> ChemicalSystem : creates
    EasyChemicalSystemGenerator --> RFEComponentLabels : uses
```

## Component Label System

The framework uses a standardized enumeration system for labeling molecular components within chemical systems [source](openfe/setup/chemicalsystem_generator/abstract_chemicalsystem_generator.py#L12-L18):

| Label | Value | Purpose |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `PROTEIN` | "protein" | Protein component in complex systems |
| `LIGAND` | "ligand" | Primary small molecule for transformation |
| `SOLVENT` | "solvent" | Solvent environment component |
